prize_parts.citation: for the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: Base editing is a simple chemical idea executed well: an engineered deaminase tethered to a programmable DNA-binding scaffold converts one base pair into another without cutting both strands. It is a genuine game-changer in the sense I use the term, completely new and already having real consequences. The cytosine and adenine base editors have been reproduced and extended by many independent laboratories, and first clinical uses are emerging. The adenine editor required evolving a deaminase for a substrate that no natural enzyme accepts, which is protein and nucleobase chemistry of real depth. Attribution is unusually clean: the conception, engineering and leadership of both editor families trace to Liu's laboratory, which fits the three-laureate ceiling without diluting the signal. It is clearly distinct from the 2020 CRISPR prize, which rewarded the programmable nuclease, not a chemical transformation of a base.
statement.case_against: The clinical benefit is still early and long-term safety (off-target and bystander editing) is not settled, so a critic can call the timing a little premature. The Nishida and Kondo cytidine deaminase fusion was reported at essentially the same time, and a single-laureate prize leaves out a credible concurrent contributor as well as the lead trainees Komor and Gaudelli. The committee may also feel that the prize sits too close to the 2020 CRISPR prize and to the wider genome-editing story, and prime editing is a separate ballot that could argue for a combined framing.

responses.point: Chabes ranks targeted protein degradation first, as the conversion of ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis into a designable chemical reaction, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa as the laureate set, and ranks base editing second.
responses.response: I agree the mechanism is well confirmed and that degraders are a real new modality, and I ranked B007 fourth myself. My reservation is attribution and maturity, not scientific merit. Eight credited names, three seats and two distinct strands (PROTACs and the thalidomide/cereblon glue mechanism) mean any trio will be contested; your set of Crews, Deshaies and Handa leaves out Ciulli's VHL ligand work, which made PROTACs drug-like, and Aili and Sparr include him. I also do not yet see an approved degrader, which is the evidence of consequences I would want. Base editing has the cleaner credit story at similar clinical maturity, but I would welcome an argument that the cereblon discovery alone is the mature core.

responses.point: Linke places massively parallel sequencing first because a chemical idea became a quantitative platform that cut the cost of reading DNA by orders of magnitude and that can be explained to a broad audience.
responses.response: I take the impact argument seriously, and I ranked B001 second; the consequences are as large as any in this list and the timing is overdue, not early. My difficulty is the one you raise yourself: three seats cover Balasubramanian, Klenerman and Rothberg, but Ju, Mayer and the cluster-amplification contributors are left out, and the split between the Solexa and 454 lineages is not obvious. I would also ask whether the committee thinks the chemistry is the decisive step. Reversible terminators are, but much of the transformative power is engineering and instrumentation. I would still call it the strongest fallback to my first choice, and I would accept it if the committee prefers a mature, unambiguous consequence over a newer discovery.

responses.point: Somfai puts Pd-catalysed C-N cross-coupling first as molecule-making at its most consequential, with Buchwald and Hartwig as a clean two-person pair and Kosugi as a precursor.
responses.response: The attribution is as clean as any here and the maturity is not in doubt, which is why I ranked it third. My hesitation is novelty. The 2010 cross-coupling prize already told the community that Pd-catalysed bond formation was recognised, and I think members who voted for it as a principle would see C-N coupling as an extension of a prized area, not a new departure. I would not call that disqualifying, since C-N coupling is a distinct and ubiquitous bond construction, but in the game-changer sense I put more weight on a capability that did not exist before. I would like to hear how you weigh the 2010 overlap against the pharmaceutical impact.

responses.point: Sparr ranks biomolecular condensates first as a general phase-behaviour principle that has reorganised cell biology, and ranks lipid nanoparticles second.
responses.response: Condensates are conceptually important and I do not dispute the community impact, but I do not rank them for a prize. I do not think it is yet clear that phase separation is the functional mechanism in living cells instead of an artefact of overexpression and in vitro droplets, and the five credited names make attribution very hard, as you note. A prize should reward what has been shown to be a game-changer and not what is still being debated. On lipid nanoparticles I am closer to you: the consequences are unmistakable, but the 2023 Medicine prize for the mRNA work complicates how a chemistry citation would be framed, and the credit between Cullis and his co-workers and the Anderson and Langer lipidoids is contested.

uncertainties: Whether Nishida and Kondo have a priority claim strong enough to require crediting them, which would push a base-editing prize to a two- or three-person set.
Whether the committee judges long-term clinical safety of base editing to be settled enough, and whether it sees the 2020 CRISPR prize as making this a second genome-editing prize.
Whether the committee prefers a mature, overdue topic (sequencing) over a newer one, and how it weighs attribution crowding for protein degradation.
Whether sequencing is viewed as chemistry or as biology and technology.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My connections are to Arieh Warshel and the Uppsala ribosome and RNA community, and none of the shortlisted candidates falls in those areas. I am a computational biochemist, so my view of base editing, sequencing and degraders is that of an informed outsider.
